title: Questions in the Temple: Authority, Caesar, and the Resurrection
summary: Teaching in the temple courts, Jesus is challenged by the chief priests, scribes, and elders about his authority, and he answers with a question about John's baptism and a parable of tenants who kill the vineyard owner's beloved son. Spies ask whether it is lawful to pay taxes to Caesar, and Sadducees pose a riddle about marriage in the resurrection. Jesus silences both, asks his own question about how the Christ can be David's son and David's Lord, and warns the disciples against the scribes' love of honor and their exploitation of widows.
story:
Jesus has entered Jerusalem as king, wept over it, cleared the temple, and taken up his post there, teaching every day (19:47-48). Luke opens this chapter by calling that teaching proclaiming the gospel (verse 1), the verb he has used for Jesus' mission since Nazareth (4:18, 4:43). The leaders who were looking for a way to destroy him now come with public questions designed to discredit him before the people or to hand him to the Roman governor. Luke follows Mark's sequence of temple debates (Mark 11:27-12:44) but leaves out the question about the greatest commandment, which he has already told in another setting (10:25-28), so that the chapter moves straight from Caesar to the resurrection to Jesus' own question.

The parable of the tenants lays bare what is happening behind the debates: the leaders of Israel are about to reject and kill the owner's beloved son. The leaders understand this at once (verse 19), and only their fear of the people keeps them from arresting him on the spot. By verse 40 no one dares to question him further, and Jesus becomes the questioner. The chapter ends with a warning about scribes who defraud widows, which leads directly into the widow's offering at the beginning of chapter 21. The threads Luke lays here run into the passion: the leaders' fear of the people returns in 22:2, the charge that Jesus forbade paying taxes to Caesar is brought to Pilate in 23:2, and Jesus' use of Psalm 110 returns at his trial, when he says that the Son of Man will be seated at the right hand of the power of God (22:69).
historical:
The chief priests, scribes, and elders of verse 1 are the three groups that made up the Sanhedrin, the council in Jerusalem that Luke later calls the council of the elders of the people (22:66). The chief priests were members of a few high priestly families, dominant under Roman rule; Luke has named Annas and Caiaphas at the start of John's ministry (3:2), and Caiaphas held the office from about AD 18 to 36. The scribes were the experts in the Law of Moses, many of them Pharisees (5:21, 5:30), and the elders were leading laymen from the great families of the city.

The Sadducees appear only here in Luke's Gospel and five times in Acts (4:1, 5:17, 23:6-8). They were a party of the priestly and lay aristocracy. Josephus says they held that the soul perishes with the body and that they rejected the traditions of the fathers that the Pharisees kept, accepting only what was written (Antiquities 13.297-298, 18.16-17; Jewish War 2.164-166), and Acts 23:8 adds that they denied angels and spirits. A later rabbinic legend traces them to Zadok, a disciple of Antigonus of Sokho, whose saying about serving God without thought of reward was taken to deny any reward after death (Avot de-Rabbi Natan A 5). The Mishnah, on the Pharisaic side of the argument, excludes from the world to come anyone who says the resurrection of the dead is not taught in the Torah (m. Sanhedrin 10:1), and the Babylonian Talmud collects rabbinic proofs of it from the five books of Moses (b. Sanhedrin 90b-92a). The Sadducees disappeared with the temple in AD 70.

The tax question was the most dangerous in the chapter. When Archelaus was deposed in AD 6, Judea became a Roman province, and the legate of Syria, Quirinius, took a census to assess its tribute (Antiquities 18.1-10). Judas the Galilean led a revolt against it, teaching that paying tribute to Rome meant accepting mortal masters in place of God (Jewish War 2.118; Acts 5:37), and Josephus traced the later revolutionary movements to him. Luke calls the tax phoros, ‘tribute’, the word Paul uses when he tells the Romans to pay taxes to whom taxes are due (Romans 13:6-7). A yes would anger many in the crowd; a no could be reported to the governor as sedition, which is exactly why the spies wanted to hand him over to the rule and authority of the governor (verse 20). The governor was Pontius Pilate (about AD 26 to 36), whose title, prefect of Judea, appears on a dedicatory stone found at Caesarea Maritima in 1961.

The denarius was a silver coin, roughly a laborer's daily wage (Matthew 20:2). The common denarius of Tiberius (emperor AD 14 to 37) bore his laureate head with the legend TI CAESAR DIVI AVG F AVGVSTVS, ‘Tiberius Caesar Augustus, son of the divine Augustus’, and on the reverse a seated woman with the title PONTIF MAXIM, ‘high priest’. The small bronze coins the prefects minted in Judea carried no portrait of the emperor (Pilate's bore Roman cult implements, a ladle and an augur's staff), so the denarius Jesus asks for was the coin of imperial tribute, carrying both a human image and a claim to divinity.

The question about David's son draws on a widespread hope. The Psalms of Solomon, written in the first century BC, pray for God to raise up the son of David to rule Israel and purge Jerusalem of Gentiles (Psalms of Solomon 17:21-25), and a scroll from Qumran reads God's promise to David in 2 Samuel 7 as a promise of the Branch of David who will arise at the end of days (4Q174, the Florilegium).
cultural:
The parable of the tenants reflects a familiar arrangement. Wealthy owners, often living elsewhere, leased vineyards to tenant farmers for a share of the harvest, and disputes were common. The Zenon papyri, the third-century BC archive of an agent of the Egyptian finance minister Apollonius, record the management of Apollonius's vineyard at Beth Anath in Galilee and trouble over its produce. A new vineyard took years to bear, and the Law forbade eating its fruit for the first three years (Leviticus 19:23-25); Luke's owner goes away ‘for a long time’ (verse 9), a detail found only here. Luke shortens the opening borrowed from Isaiah's Song of the Vineyard (Isaiah 5:1-7) that Mark keeps in full, but his hearers would still know that the vineyard of the LORD of Hosts is the house of Israel (Isaiah 5:7). Beating, shaming, and sending away empty-handed were ordinary ways of refusing payment; in Luke no servant is killed until the son comes.

The saying about the stone draws on several images at once. Psalm 118, the last of the Hallel psalms sung at the pilgrim feasts, had just been on the disciples' lips at the entry (19:38), and its twenty-second verse speaks of a stone the builders rejected. In Hebrew the words for son (ben) and stone (even) sound alike, which may have made the psalm a natural sequel to a parable about a son. Verse 18 adds the stone of stumbling that breaks those who fall over it (Isaiah 8:14-15) and the stone cut without hands that crushes the kingdoms in Nebuchadnezzar's dream (Daniel 2:34-35, 2:44-45). A later rabbinic proverb says the same thing in homely terms: if the stone falls on the pot, woe to the pot, and if the pot falls on the stone, woe to the pot (Esther Rabbah 7:10).

The Sadducees' question rests on levirate marriage (Deuteronomy 25:5-10): if a man died childless, his brother was to marry the widow, and the first son counted as the dead man's, so that his name and inheritance would continue (compare Genesis 38 and Ruth 4). Their seven brothers may parody two Jewish stories they knew: Sarah in Tobit, who lost seven husbands (Tobit 3:8), and the seven brothers of 2 Maccabees 7, who died under Antiochus IV confessing that God would raise them. Jesus' answer uses ideas already present in Jewish thought. In 1 Enoch 15:6-7 God tells the fallen Watchers that as spiritual and immortal beings they were given no wives, since wives were given to mortals so that their line would continue. Second Baruch 51:10 says the righteous raised will be made like the angels. A saying of Rav in the Talmud holds that in the world to come there is no eating, drinking, or procreation, but the righteous sit with crowns on their heads enjoying the radiance of the divine presence (b. Berakhot 17a). And 4 Maccabees speaks of the patriarchs Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob as living to God (4 Maccabees 7:19, 16:25), close to Luke's added line that to him all are alive (verse 38).

The scribes' long robes (stolai) were marks of learned status; greetings in the marketplace meant being hailed with titles of respect; the chief seats in the synagogue faced the congregation; and the places of honor at banquets were the couches nearest the host. Jesus had made the same charge against Pharisees at a meal (11:43). How the scribes defrauded widows of their houses is not stated; suggestions include charging for legal help, mismanaging estates they held in trust, and exploiting the hospitality of devout women. The Law made widows the special concern of God (Exodus 22:22-24, Deuteronomy 24:17), and the prophets condemned those who made widows their prey (Isaiah 10:2).
literary:
The chapter is a sequence of controversy dialogues, a form common in Jewish and Greek teaching, in which a hostile question is put, a trap is set, and the answer turns the trap back on the questioner. Luke arranges them in six steps: a question about authority met with a counter-question (1-8), a parable with its scriptural sequel (9-19), a political trap (20-26), a theological trap (27-40), Jesus' own question (41-44), and a public warning (45-47). The word exousia, ‘authority’, frames the first half: the leaders ask by what authority Jesus acts (verse 2), he refuses to tell them (verse 8), and the spies hope to hand him to the authority of the governor (verse 20). Each round ends with the opponents silenced, first by refusing to answer (verse 7), then by amazement (verse 26), and finally by fear to ask anything more (verse 40).

Luke shapes Mark's material in small but telling ways. The parable is addressed to the people (verse 9), not only to the leaders, and the people respond to its ending with “May such a thing never happen!” (verse 16), recoiling from the thought of the vineyard given to others. Only Luke has the owner deliberate aloud, ‘What shall I do?’, and add ‘perhaps’ (isōs, found only here in the New Testament), and only Luke says Jesus looked directly at them before quoting the psalm (verse 17). In Luke the spies pretend to be righteous (dikaioi, verse 20), and Jesus perceives their craftiness (panourgia, verse 23), where Mark speaks of hypocrisy. Luke's answer to the Sadducees is longer than Mark's, contrasting the sons of this age with those considered worthy of the age to come (verses 34-36), and it ends with a line only Luke has: “for to Him all are alive” (verse 38). Some of the scribes, Pharisees who shared Jesus' belief in the resurrection, then approve (verse 39), a scene that anticipates Paul dividing the council by appealing to the resurrection (Acts 23:6-9).

The sequence moves from Jesus as the object of questions to Jesus as the one who asks, and from the leaders' private reckoning (verses 5-6, 14) to Jesus' public warning (verse 45). The last line about scribes who defraud widows is set immediately beside the widow who gives all she has (21:1-4), and the two scenes are meant to be read together.

outline.t: The parable of the tenants and the rejected stone

doctrines.note: In the parable Jesus is the owner's beloved son, distinct from all the servants sent before him, and the rejected stone God makes the cornerstone. With Psalm 110:1 he asks how the Christ can be both David's son and David's Lord. The Messiah is more than a restored Davidic king; he is the one David's God seats at his right hand (22:69, Acts 2:34-36).

The coin bearing Caesar's image may be given back to Caesar, since rulers have a real but limited claim (compare Romans 13:6-7). The things of God belong to God, and human beings, made in God's image (Genesis 1:27), owe him themselves. Jesus neither endorses revolt nor grants Caesar the divinity his coin claimed.

Against the Sadducees Jesus affirms the resurrection of the dead. Those considered worthy of the age to come can no longer die; they are sons of God because they are sons of the resurrection. Resurrection life is not this life resumed with its arrangements intact but a new mode of life by the power of the God to whom all are alive.

The parable tells Israel's history with God, the vineyard he planted and the servants he sent, and its climax in the rejection of his son. The judgment falls on the tenants, the leaders who knew the parable was aimed at them (verse 19), and the vineyard is not destroyed but given to others. How Luke sees Israel's future is debated; see the hard question below.

Jesus warns against religious leaders who love public honor while they defraud widows of their houses and cover it with long prayers, and he says they will receive greater condemnation (verse 47). God holds those with religious authority to a stricter account for how they treat the vulnerable.

words.note: Exousia, authority, the right and power to act. It occurs about 102 times in the New Testament and 16 in Luke, four in this chapter. Luke has shown Jesus teaching with authority (4:32) and claiming authority to forgive sins (5:24); the devil claimed that authority over the kingdoms of the world had been given to him (4:6); and at the arrest Jesus will say that this hour belongs to the power (exousia) of darkness (22:53). The leaders' question about who gave Jesus authority is the question the whole Gospel answers.

Agapētos, beloved, often with the sense of only or uniquely dear. It occurs about 61 times in the New Testament but only twice in Luke: the voice at the baptism, “You are My beloved Son” (3:22), and the owner's words here (verse 13). The Greek Old Testament uses it for Isaac, Abraham's only son (Genesis 22:2). Its appearance in the parable links the owner's son with the Son named from heaven.

Phoros, tribute, the tax paid by a subject people to a ruling power. It occurs five times in the New Testament: here (verse 22), in the charge before Pilate that Jesus forbade paying it (23:2), and three times in Romans 13:6-7, where Paul tells believers to pay it. Mark and Matthew use kēnsos, from the Latin census; Luke's word is the ordinary Greek term his readers would know.

Eikōn, image, likeness. It occurs about 23 times in the New Testament, once in Luke (verse 24). It is the word of the Greek Old Testament in Genesis 1:26-27, where God makes humanity according to his image. Jesus' question about whose image is on the coin invites the hearer to ask whose image he bears, and Paul later calls Christ the image of God (2 Corinthians 4:4, Colossians 1:15).

Anastasis, resurrection, literally a standing up. It occurs about 42 times in the New Testament and six in Luke: Simeon's prophecy of the falling and rising of many (2:34), the resurrection of the righteous (14:14), and four times in this debate. It refers to the bodily raising of the dead at the end of the age, the hope of Daniel 12:2 and 2 Maccabees 7, which the Sadducees denied. In Acts it becomes the center of the apostles' preaching about Jesus (Acts 4:2, 17:18).

Isangelos, like or equal to the angels. The word occurs only here in the New Testament (verse 36) and is very rare anywhere in Greek. Luke explains its meaning in the same sentence: the risen can no longer die. The likeness is to the angels' immortality, not a claim that the raised become angels or lose their bodies. The point answers the Sadducees on two counts at once, since they denied both resurrection and angels (Acts 23:8).

Kurios, lord, master, and in the Greek Old Testament the ordinary rendering of the divine name YHWH. It occurs more than seven hundred times in the New Testament. In Psalm 110:1, quoted in verse 42, it stands twice: first for YHWH, then for the Hebrew adoni, ‘my lord’, a title for a superior. Jesus' question turns on the second: a father does not call his son lord, so David's Lord must be more than David's descendant. In verse 37 it names God at the burning bush.

Chēra, widow. It occurs about 26 times in the New Testament, nine of them in Luke, more than any other Gospel: Anna (2:37), the widow of Zarephath (4:25-26), the widow of Nain (7:12), the persistent widow (18:3-5), the widows whose houses the scribes devour (verse 47), and the widow at the treasury (21:2-3). In the Law and the prophets the widow, with the orphan and the stranger, is the test of a people's justice, and Luke keeps her in view to the end.

christ:
Jesus reveals his identity in this chapter more openly than at any point since the baptism. In the parable, after many servants have been beaten and sent away empty, the owner decides to send his beloved son, the phrase of the voice from heaven at the baptism (3:22). The son is not one more messenger but the heir, and the tenants kill him precisely because he is the heir. In Luke and Matthew the son is first thrown out of the vineyard and then killed, which Christian readers have long connected with Jesus' death outside the city (Hebrews 13:12). Jesus thus tells the men who will arrange his death that he knows what they intend and who he is.

The quotation of Psalm 118:22 adds what the parable alone could not: the son killed and thrown out is the stone the builders rejected, and God makes him the cornerstone. Peter will say exactly this to the same council after the resurrection (Acts 4:10-11), and 1 Peter builds a whole picture of the church as a spiritual house on that stone (1 Peter 2:4-8). Verse 18 warns that the stone cannot be treated as neutral: those who stumble over it are broken, and those on whom it falls are crushed, the stone of Daniel 2 that becomes a kingdom filling the earth.

In the debates Jesus shows himself the true interpreter of Scripture and the true image of God. The coin bears Caesar's image; human beings bear God's; and Jesus, whom Paul calls the image of the invisible God (Colossians 1:15), will give himself wholly to God. He answers the Sadducees from God's self-naming at the burning bush: the God who calls himself the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob long after their deaths is the God of the living, and within days his own resurrection will be the first fruits of the life he defends (1 Corinthians 15:20). Those who share in it are called sons of God because they are sons of the resurrection (verse 36), language Paul uses for Jesus himself, declared Son of God with power by his resurrection from the dead (Romans 1:4).

Finally, Jesus asks how David can call his own descendant Lord. Psalm 110:1 became the Old Testament text the New Testament cites or echoes more than any other, because it speaks of one seated at God's right hand until his enemies are subdued. Luke answers the question in his own story: at his trial Jesus says that from now on the Son of Man will be seated at the right hand of the power of God (22:69), and at Pentecost Peter quotes the same psalm to declare that God has made Jesus both Lord and Christ (Acts 2:34-36). He is David's son by descent (1:32, 18:38) and David's Lord by exaltation.
interpretation:
The parable of the tenants was read by the church fathers as a summary of salvation history. Irenaeus (Against Heresies 4.36.1-2) set it out in full: God planted the vineyard in the patriarchs, let it out under the law of Moses, sent the prophets, then his Son, and gave the vineyard to others. That reading, repeated for centuries, often slid into the claim that God had rejected the Jewish people and replaced them with the church. After the Holocaust, Christian scholars such as Rosemary Radford Ruether (Faith and Fratricide, 1974) traced Christian contempt for Jews to such readings, and the Second Vatican Council's declaration Nostra Aetate (1965) taught that Jews should not be presented as rejected or accursed by God, as if this followed from Scripture. Modern critical study asked whether Jesus told allegories at all; the discovery of the Gospel of Thomas at Nag Hammadi in 1945, whose saying 65 gives a shorter version followed by the rejected stone (saying 66), sharpened the debate, and Klyne Snodgrass (The Parable of the Wicked Tenants, 1983) argued that the parable with its allegorical features goes back to Jesus. On Israel in Luke-Acts, Jacob Jervell (Luke and the People of God, 1972) argued that Luke sees Israel divided, not rejected, and Robert Tannehill (Journal of Biblical Literature, 1985) read the story of Israel in Luke-Acts as a tragedy that Luke grieves.

The tax saying has a long political history. Justin Martyr (First Apology 17) cited it to assure the emperor that Christians paid their taxes while worshiping God alone. Tertullian (On Idolatry 15) drew the image argument that preachers still use: give Caesar the coin that bears his image, and give God yourself, since you bear his. Medieval disputes between popes and emperors, Luther's treatise on Temporal Authority (1523), and modern debates about church and state all appealed to it, and ‘render unto Caesar’, from the King James Version, became an English proverb. Titian's The Tribute Money (1516, now in Dresden) is among the earliest paintings of the scene.

The resurrection debate mattered to synagogue and church alike. The Mishnah's ruling against those who deny that the Torah teaches resurrection (m. Sanhedrin 10:1) and the second blessing of the Amidah, prayed daily, which praises God who gives life to the dead, show that the Pharisaic side won in Judaism. Augustine (City of God 22.17) used the verse to argue that both men and women will rise in their own sex, with marriage and desire no longer in view but nature preserved. The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints reads the verse differently: its Doctrine and Covenants (section 132, dated 1843) teaches that those who are not sealed in eternal marriage in this life neither marry nor are given in marriage in the next. Verses 27 to 38 are read in November of Year C in the Revised Common Lectionary (Proper 27) and the Roman lectionary (Thirty-second Sunday in Ordinary Time), often near All Saints and the commemoration of the dead.

Psalm 110 has a double reception. The New Testament reads it of Christ's exaltation; Justin Martyr reports Jewish teachers of his day applying it to Hezekiah (Dialogue with Trypho 33, 83); the Babylonian Talmud (Nedarim 32b) and Rashi read it of Abraham; and David Hay (Glory at the Right Hand, 1973) traced its many uses in early Christianity.
text:
English Bibles differ at a few points in this chapter. In verse 13 the King James Version reads ‘it may be they will reverence him when they see him’, adding ‘when they see him’ from later manuscripts. In verse 23 it adds Jesus' question ‘Why tempt ye me?’, which is absent from Codex Sinaiticus, Codex Vaticanus, and other early witnesses and was probably borrowed from Mark 12:15 and Matthew 22:18. In verse 30 the King James Version reads ‘And the second took her to wife, and he died childless’, where the earliest manuscripts have only ‘and the second’, which is why the BSB's verse 30 consists of three words. The King James Version's ‘Shew me a penny’ in verse 24 is a translation choice, not a textual one: it rendered denarius by the smallest silver coin English readers knew.

Verse 18 has a textual echo elsewhere. The same saying appears in Matthew 21:44, but that verse is missing from Codex Bezae, minuscule 33, several Old Latin manuscripts, and the Sinaitic Syriac, and many editors think it was added to Matthew from Luke; others keep it as original to Matthew. Some modern Bibles print Matthew 21:44 in brackets or a note for this reason. In Luke the verse is secure.

In verse 43 Luke quotes Psalm 110:1 exactly as the Greek Old Testament has it, ‘a footstool for your feet’, where Mark's earliest manuscripts read ‘under your feet’ (Mark 12:36). Psalm 110 is Psalm 109 in the Greek and Latin numbering. In verse 37 Luke's wording, that Moses calls the Lord the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, follows Exodus 3:6 and 3:15, where God names himself that way.

teach.big: Jesus answers every challenge to his authority by revealing who he is, the beloved Son and rejected stone, the image of God's claim, the Lord of the living, and David's Lord, and he calls his hearers to give God what is God's.

outline.t: Those who will not answer honestly about God's work in John cannot receive the truth about Jesus' authority; evasion closes the door.
God has been patient with his people through servant after servant and finally sends his beloved Son; rejecting the Son is rejecting the owner.
The rejected stone becomes the cornerstone; no one can stay neutral before Jesus, and God overturns the builders' verdict.
Give Caesar his coin, but give God yourself; the state's claim is real and limited, and God's claim on those who bear his image is total.
Scoffers can build clever cases against the resurrection by imagining the age to come as this age extended.
The resurrection life is new, deathless, and belongs to those counted worthy; the God of the patriarchs is the God of the living.
The Christ is David's son and David's Lord; Scripture itself points beyond a merely human king to the one enthroned at God's right hand.
Religious status, public honor, and long prayers can cover the exploitation of the vulnerable, and God judges religious leaders more strictly.

teach.pitfalls:
The tax saying is often used to support a sharp separation of religion from politics, as if Caesar and God had separate territories that never overlap. Jesus' second clause claims everything for God, including the one who pays the tax. The opposite misuse makes the saying a slogan for either civil obedience at any cost or for tax resistance; the saying is more pointed than either, and Luke shows that the leaders later lied about it (23:2).

The parable of the tenants has often been preached as God's rejection of the Jewish people. Luke says the leaders knew it was spoken against them (verse 19), the people recoiled from its ending (verse 16), and the vineyard itself is not destroyed. Preach it as a warning to all who hold God's people in trust, church leaders included.

The Sadducees' question is sometimes answered with speculation about what heaven will be like, or with the popular idea that the dead become angels. Jesus says the raised are like the angels in one respect, that they can no longer die, and he bases the hope on the character of God, not on details of the afterlife. The warning about the scribes is easily turned into a caricature of Jews or of Pharisees; Luke says some scribes approved Jesus' answer (verse 39), and the warning applies to every religious professional who loves honor more than the people entrusted to him.
teach.pastoral: The Sadducees' question about a woman married seven times will press on widows and widowers, on people who have remarried after a spouse's death, and on those whose marriages were painful. Some fear losing their spouse forever; others are relieved to hear that marriage as they knew it will not continue. Both need to hear that Jesus does not say love or recognition ends, but that the raised can no longer die and live wholly to God. Be careful not to promise more than Scripture says, and not to dismiss real grief with a proof text. The warning about those who defraud widows may speak to people who have been financially exploited by religious leaders; it tells them God sees and judges it.

hard.q: Does the parable of the tenants teach that God rejected Israel and gave its place to the church?
hard.a:
The objection is grounded in the text and in its history. The owner comes and destroys the tenants and gives the vineyard to others (verse 16), and the vineyard in Isaiah 5 is Israel. For centuries Christian preaching read the parable as the story of God's rejection of the Jews: Irenaeus (Against Heresies 4.36.1-2) already set out the allegory ending with the vineyard given to the Gentile church, and the destruction of Jerusalem was presented as the owner's punishment. Jewish readers and many Christian scholars since the Holocaust have argued that this reading made the parable an engine of contempt; Rosemary Radford Ruether (Faith and Fratricide, 1974) argued that anti-Judaism grew out of the church's christological reading of Israel's story. On this view, whatever Jesus meant, the parable as the Gospels tell it teaches supersession, the replacement of Israel by the church.

The responses begin with Luke's own framing. Jesus tells the parable to the people (verse 9), and it is the scribes and chief priests who realize that he has spoken it against them (verse 19); the tenants are the leaders, not the nation. The people's response, “May such a thing never happen!” (verse 16), shows them siding with the vineyard, not with its destruction. The vineyard itself is not uprooted, as in Isaiah 5, but given to others, and Luke's story names those others: the Twelve, all Jews, to whom Jesus gives a kingdom so that they will sit on thrones judging the twelve tribes of Israel (22:29-30). In Acts thousands of Jews in Jerusalem believe (Acts 2:41, 4:4, 21:20), and Jacob Jervell (Luke and the People of God, 1972) argued that Luke presents Israel as divided by the gospel, not replaced. Robert Tannehill (Journal of Biblical Literature, 1985) read Luke-Acts as telling Israel's story as a tragedy that Luke grieves rather than celebrates, and Luke's hope for Israel's restoration (Acts 1:6, 3:19-21) is still open at the end of Acts. The Second Vatican Council (Nostra Aetate, 1965) and many Protestant bodies have rejected the teaching that the Jews are rejected by God. Interpreters still differ on how Luke sees the future of the Jewish people as a whole; what the parable itself indicts is leadership that treats God's vineyard as its own.

hard.q: If there is no marriage in the resurrection, what happens to the love between husbands and wives?
hard.a:
The objection has force for anyone who has loved a spouse. Jesus appears to say that the most intimate human bond ends at death, which can sound like a loss rather than a promise. Others press it from a different side: the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints teaches that marriages sealed by proper authority continue eternally, and it reads this verse as describing only those who were not so sealed (Doctrine and Covenants 132:15-17). Jewish tradition also held varied views; a saying of Rav describes the world to come as without eating, drinking, or procreation (b. Berakhot 17a), while other rabbinic texts picture its joys in bodily terms.

Jesus is answering a specific question: whose legal wife will the widow be. Marriage in this age is bound up with death; the levirate law the Sadducees cite existed to carry a dead man's name and inheritance beyond death through children. In the age to come, Jesus says, the raised can no longer die (verse 36), so that function ends. He says they are like the angels in that respect, not that they become angels or cease to be embodied persons, and he does not say that love or recognition ends. Augustine (City of God 22.17) argued that both men and women rise as themselves, and many theologians since have held that the exclusive covenant of marriage gives way to something fuller rather than emptier, with the love learned in marriage completed in the marriage of Christ and his people, which Revelation calls the wedding supper of the Lamb (Revelation 19:7-9). Those who read the verse the Latter-day Saint way and those who read it the historic Christian way disagree about the church's authority as much as about the verse. Scripture says little in detail about relationships in the resurrection, and readers do well to hold their conclusions with restraint while trusting the God to whom all are alive.

observe: What question do the leaders ask in verse 2, and why can they not answer Jesus' counter-question in verses 3 and 4?
In the parable, what happens to each servant and to the son? What does the owner say before sending the son?
What two things does Jesus say about the raised in verses 35 and 36, and what passage of Moses does he use to prove the resurrection?
interpret: Why does Jesus follow the parable with Psalm 118:22? What does the image of the stone add to the story of the son?
